clue.text: Looking for an overshoe? Look in the cleft

indicators.note: 'in' tells us one piece sits inside the other, the look-word placed within the cleft

parts.note: a cleft is a gash, a split or crack
'lo' is an old exclamation meaning look!

explanation.surface: A shopper hunting for a rubber overshoe is told to peer into a crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looking for' is the question's opening, not wordplay; 'Look' is the old exclamation 'lo!', as in 'lo and behold'.
explanation.definitionFit: A galosh is a waterproof rubber shoe worn over an ordinary one in wet weather.

clue.text: Game commendation for stolen merchandise

parts.note: goods are merchandise
hot is slang for stolen

explanation.surface: Praise for a sporting effort is likened to stolen merchandise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' is the shooting of game birds: praise for a hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Praise called out to a marksman who brings down a bird is a shooting compliment.

clue.text: What survives must be finished with Labour

parts.note: the Labour Party is on the political left
over means finished

explanation.surface: A political comment that whatever lasts must end with Labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' is the British left-wing party, so it gives LEFT; 'finished' is OVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A remnant that remains after the rest is used up is what survives.

clue.text: Celebrity going to church needs a stiffener

parts.note: a star is a celebrity

explanation.surface: A famous person going to church needs a drink to steady the nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stiffener' suggests a stiff drink; here it is the laundry stuff that stiffens collars.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch is used in laundry to stiffen fabric, so it is a stiffening agent.

clue.text: A station carriage

explanation.surface: A railway station and a horse-drawn vehicle share one name.
explanation.walkthrough: VICTORIA is a major London railway terminus, and also a light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage named after the queen.
explanation.definitionFit: London's Victoria terminus is a railway station; a victoria is also a low four-wheeled horse-drawn coach for two.

clue.text: Bird to be found in a Carib island

indicators.note: 'to be found in' says the letters are tucked away in the words that follow

explanation.surface: A bird lives on a Caribbean island.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibis is a long-billed wading bird.

clue.text: Got there somehow, in concert

indicators.note: somehow means in some unstated way, so the letters of got there are rearranged

explanation.surface: People got to a concert one way or another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' signals an anagram of GOT THERE.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in concert means acting jointly, all at once as a group.

clue.text: It harboured the Colossus

parts.note: the giant ancient statue said to stand astride a harbour on a Greek island

explanation.surface: A place that housed a giant statue.
explanation.walkthrough: The Colossus, one of the Seven Wonders, stood by the harbour of this Greek island; 'harboured' plays on that.
explanation.definitionFit: The Colossus was a huge bronze statue of the sun god set up at the harbour of this Aegean island.

clue.text: Let us leave the emperor for a month

indicators.note: 'Let us leave' tells us the letters of us go away from the emperor's name

parts.note: Augustus was the first Roman emperor

explanation.surface: Let us abandon the emperor for a month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' removes US from AUGUSTUS.
explanation.definitionFit: August is the eighth month of the year, named after that Roman emperor.

clue.text: If you have one; you are'not at your best

definitions.text: If you have one; you are'not at your best

parts.words: If you have one; you are'not at your best
parts.note: the whole clue describes a day when a person performs below their usual standard

explanation.surface: Everyone has days when they are not on form.
explanation.definitionFit: A day when you perform poorly is an informal idiom for a bad, below-par day.

clue.text: Keenly contested, and sound 45 a bell

explanation.surface: A fierce contest is likened to the ring of a bell.
explanation.walkthrough: A ding-dong battle is a hard-fought one; 'ding-dong' is also the noise a bell makes. The '45' is scan debris for 'as' or 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiercely fought argument or match is called a ding-dong; the same word imitates a ringing bell's chime.

clue.text: All -right on shore, but unpopular in the kitchen

explanation.surface: Something welcome at the seaside is resented in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: A breaker is a wave crashing on the shore, harmless there; a breaker of crockery is unwelcome in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A wave breaking on the beach is one sense; someone who smashes dishes is the other.

clue.text: A small ad, has crowd in confusion

indicators.note: letters in confusion are jumbled, so the words has and crowd are rearranged

explanation.surface: A little advertisement draws a muddled crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in confusion' signals an anagram of HAS plus CROWD.
explanation.definitionFit: A showcard is a card displayed in a shop window to advertise something, a small advertisement.

clue.text: The accent aboard is very French

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'The accent aboard is very French (6)': the only parse reads 'aboard' as 'in SS', so the one word is both the container indicator and the SS letters, which the check refuses.
annotationWithheld.clue: The accent aboard is very French

clue.text: The remedy is for dad to bring in a winner

indicators.note: bringing in means taking something inside, so dad surrounds the winner

parts.note: pa is dad
an ace is a winner, as at tennis

explanation.surface: A father hopes a winning bet will cure everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a winner' gives AN ACE, which 'to bring in' puts inside PA.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea is a cure-all, a single remedy for every ill.

clue.text: Verbal admission

parts.note: a spoken form of words that gets you admitted, like the magic password in the tale of Ali Baba

explanation.surface: Someone confesses something out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admission' looks like a confession, but here it means being let in, by the password from Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Arabian Nights story the cave opens to a spoken password, so it is admission granted by words.

clue.text: Pecuniary reparation for mother is growing old

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother
ages means grows old

explanation.surface: Compensation is claimed on behalf of an ageing mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Damages are a sum of money awarded by a court as compensation for loss or injury.

clue.text: Comfortable seat for the, amateur

explanation.surface: A comfy chair suits a non-professional.
explanation.walkthrough: An armchair critic or general is an amateur who theorises without practical experience.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy chair with arms is one sense; as an adjective it means non-professional, theorising from a distance.

clue.text: It is all up with the hammer, kop, but it keeps you dry

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'It is all up with the hammer, kop, but it keeps you dry (8)'. 'hammer, kop' looks garbled by OCR; no parse gives UMBRELLA and a search found no source.
annotationWithheld.clue: It is all up with the hammer, kop, but it keeps you dry

clue.text: Feelers for advance payment upset 'the Princess

parts.note: an ante is a stake paid in advance in poker

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the princess's name is jumbled

parts.note: Princess Anne, the Princess Royal

explanation.surface: Sensors for an upfront payment unsettle a royal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' scrambles the Princess Royal's name, the British princess known in crosswords as Anne, and those letters follow the poker stake.
explanation.definitionFit: Antennae are the sensory feelers on an insect's head.

clue.text: Magazine team

explanation.surface: A publication shares its name with a sports side.
explanation.walkthrough: An arsenal is a store of weapons, a magazine in the military sense; ARSENAL is also a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: A magazine in the military sense is a weapons store, as is an arsenal; Arsenal is also a famous football club.

clue.text: No one is coming back — it is a bad sign

indicators.note: coming back means the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: nemo is Latin for no one

explanation.surface: When nobody returns, it bodes ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is coming back' turns NEMO (Latin for 'no one') round.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent, often of trouble, is a sign of things to come.

clue.text: One who utters a'coin

explanation.surface: A speaker and a coin share a name.
explanation.walkthrough: A stater is one who states; it was also an ancient Greek coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who says something states it; the stater was an ancient Greek gold or silver coin.

clue.text: "How now, you black, and midnight hags" (Macbeth)

definitions.text: "How now, you black, and midnight hags" (Macbeth)

parts.words: "How now, you black, and midnight hags" (Macbeth)
parts.note: Macbeth's greeting to the witches has a word missing, an adjective for their hidden doings

explanation.surface: Macbeth greets the witches.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line is Macbeth's greeting to the three witches, with one adjective left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth calls the witches covert, clandestine hags, using the word for something kept hidden.

clue.text: Nymph deserted by. Paris

parts.note: in Greek myth the Trojan prince left his mountain nymph wife for Helen

explanation.surface: A nymph is abandoned by her lover from Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paris' is the Trojan prince, not the French city: he left this nymph of Mount Ida for Helen.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the mountain nymph of Ida was the first wife of the Trojan prince, abandoned for Helen.

clue.text: Three in sequence start a row with the Church of England

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Three things in order begin a quarrel with the established church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start' links the definition to the wordplay; a tierce is a run of three cards of one suit in piquet.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games such as piquet a run of three cards of one suit in order is called a tierce.

clue.text: Practise about what people are dying to ride in

parts.note: re means about or concerning

parts.words: what people are dying to ride in
parts.note: a hearse carries the dead, so it is the vehicle people are dying to ride in

explanation.surface: Someone practises by talking about a vehicle everyone longs to ride in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dying to' looks like 'eager to', but it means literally dead: the funeral car.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehearse is to practise a play or performance before giving it.

clue.text: Can you spare a coin ?

parts.note: echoes the Depression-era song title Brother, Can You Spare... with the small coin left out

explanation.surface: A beggar asks for change.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'Brother, Can You Spare a ...' asks for a ten-cent US coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A ten-cent piece is a small US coin, the one asked for in the Depression song.

clue.text: Tortoise put quietly in the ground

indicators.note: 'put in' says the quiet letter goes inside the word for ground

parts.note: terrain is ground or land
p (piano) is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: A tortoise is quietly buried in the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts P inside TERRAIN. A terrapin is a freshwater turtle, loosely a tortoise.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrapin is a small freshwater turtle, a shelled reptile of the same family group as a tortoise.

clue.text: "No -., or swart faery of the mine" (Milton)

definitions.text: "No -., or swart faery of the mine" (Milton)

parts.words: "No -., or swart faery of the mine" (Milton)
parts.note: a line from Milton's masque Comus with one word missing, a creature to set beside the dark fairy of the mine

explanation.surface: A quotation from Milton about mischievous spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Milton's Comus: the missing word names a small mischievous sprite.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in Milton's line names a mischievous sprite of folklore, paired with a dark fairy of the mines.

clue.text: Came back from a short walk in the grass

indicators.note: 'in' places the short walk inside the grass

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass
a turn is a short stroll

explanation.surface: Someone returned from a brief stroll through the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' links definition and wordplay; a turn in the sense of a short stroll, as in 'a turn round the garden'.
explanation.definitionFit: Returned means came back, arrived home again.

clue.text: See 15
